explanations.explanation: Judgment is the word. God presides in the divine assembly, and among the gods He renders judgment (Psalm 82:1). Nobody in that room got to wander in late and grab a seat in the back. This is a court, and God is the one running it.

Blessings sound nice, friend, like a batch fresh out of the oven. But the verse says God renders judgment among the gods (Psalm 82:1). This assembly is more courtroom than cookie party. The next verses show why.

No gift bags in this assembly, friend. The verse says God presides in the divine assembly and renders judgment among the gods (Psalm 82:1). I bet everybody in that room was thinking about what was coming, not what they'd get.

explanations.answer: Judging unjustly and favoring the wicked
explanations.explanation: That's it. God asks, "How long will you judge unjustly and show partiality to the wicked?" (Psalm 82:2). Notice He says "How long," so this has been going on a while. A judge who plays favorites is like a scale that always leans the same way. You can't trust the number it gives you.

explanations.answer: Ignoring the feasts and the sacrifices
explanations.explanation: Good guess if you were thinking religious duties, but that's not in this verse. God asks, "How long will you judge unjustly and show partiality to the wicked?" (Psalm 82:2). The complaint is about how they judge. It's about justice, friend, not a missed calendar.

explanations.answer: Refusing to hear any cases at all
explanations.explanation: These judges are hearing cases, friend. That's the problem. God asks, "How long will you judge unjustly and show partiality to the wicked?" (Psalm 82:2). They're showing up to work and getting the verdicts crooked.
Right on. God says, "Defend the cause of the weak and fatherless…" (Psalm 82:3). These are the folks with nobody to stand up for them in a room like that. God tells the judges to be the ones who do.

The king and his officials already have plenty of people in their corner, friend. God says, "Defend the cause of the weak and fatherless…" (Psalm 82:3). He points the judges toward the ones with nobody speaking up for them.

Not this time. The verse says, "Defend the cause of the weak and fatherless…" (Psalm 82:3). Priests and Levites don't show up in this psalm at all. God's focus is on the people who have no one to speak for them.
True. God says, "…uphold the rights of the afflicted and oppressed." (Psalm 82:3). It's the same job said a second way. Defend the weak, and also hold up the rights of the ones being pressed down.

It's true, friend. The verse says, "Defend the cause of the weak and fatherless; uphold the rights of the afflicted and oppressed." (Psalm 82:3). God gives the judges two jobs in one breath, and this is the second one.

explanations.answer: All the foundations of the earth
explanations.explanation: That's the one. The verse says, "…all the foundations of the earth are shaken." (Psalm 82:5). Wandering in the darkness and shaken foundations in the same breath. I think that's a house with no light and no floor you can trust, and that's a rough combo.

Jerusalem's walls aren't mentioned anywhere in this psalm, friend. The verse says, "…all the foundations of the earth are shaken." (Psalm 82:5). It's the whole earth's foundations here. That's way bigger than one city.

Thrones sound like a smart guess, since rulers are in this psalm. But the verse says, "…all the foundations of the earth are shaken." (Psalm 82:5). It doesn't name thrones. It's the foundations of the whole earth.

explanations.answer: Gods and sons of the Most High
explanations.explanation: Yes. God says, "I have said, 'You are gods; you are all sons of the Most High.'" (Psalm 82:6). That's a big title to be handed. And it makes the verdict in the next verse hit even harder.
Those are real roles in the Bible, but they're not in this verse. God says, "I have said, 'You are gods; you are all sons of the Most High.'" (Psalm 82:6). That's what He reminds them He called them.

explanations.answer: Priests and servants of the temple
explanations.explanation: Close to the Bible's world, friend, but not in this verse. God says, "I have said, 'You are gods; you are all sons of the Most High.'" (Psalm 82:6). Those are the titles He reminds them of.
Right. God says, "But like mortals you will die…" (Psalm 82:7). The ones He called gods are told they'll die like mortals. That's a short sentence, but I bet it landed like a dropped tray.

explanations.answer: They will be scattered among the nations
explanations.explanation: Scattering isn't what the verse says. God says, "But like mortals you will die…" (Psalm 82:7). It's about death, friend, not being sent off to other places.

explanations.answer: They will be turned into servants
explanations.explanation: Not servants, friend. The verse says, "But like mortals you will die…" (Psalm 82:7). God isn't handing out new jobs here. He's telling them how it ends for them.
True. God says, "…and like rulers you will fall." (Psalm 82:7). Two comparisons in one verse. They die like mortals and fall like rulers. A title can sound grand, but it doesn't keep anyone standing.
It's true, friend. The verse says, "But like mortals you will die, and like rulers you will fall." (Psalm 82:7). God gives them both lines in the same verse.
Not quite. The psalm says, "Arise, O God, judge the earth, for all the nations are Your inheritance." (Psalm 82:8). It asks God to judge the earth, not one nation. That's a much bigger courtroom.
False is right. The psalm says, "Arise, O God, judge the earth, for all the nations are Your inheritance." (Psalm 82:8). The ask covers the whole earth. Israel isn't named in this verse at all.

explanations.answer: All the nations are His inheritance
explanations.explanation: You got it. The psalm says, "…for all the nations are Your inheritance." (Psalm 82:8). That's the reason it gives. The psalm ends by calling God to arise, with all the nations as His.

explanations.answer: The rulers have all stepped down
explanations.explanation: Nothing in the psalm says that, friend. The reason is "…for all the nations are Your inheritance." (Psalm 82:8). The rulers are told they'll fall in verse 7, but the closing prayer gives a different reason.

explanations.answer: The nations have asked Him to
explanations.explanation: The psalm never says the nations asked. It says, "Arise, O God, judge the earth, for all the nations are Your inheritance." (Psalm 82:8). The reason given is that they belong to Him.
